facts.statement: Fossils of Necrosuchus were discovered on April 3, 1931, during the First Scarritt Expedition in Argentina.
facts.quote: The fossil remains of Necrosuchus were unearthed on April 3, 1931 during the First Scarritt Expedition in the Argentinian Salamanca Formation

facts.statement: The genus Necrosuchus was first described by George G. Simpson in 1937.
facts.quote: He eventually published his preliminary description in 1937

facts.statement: Detailed descriptions of the postcranial skeleton of Necrosuchus were not published until 2012.
facts.quote: the postcranial was not described until 2012

facts.statement: The name Necrosuchus combines the Greek words for 'dead' and 'crocodile', inspired by a question from a well-meaning lady.
facts.quote: Simpson explains the meaning of the generic name as being a compound word of "nekros" meaning "dead," and "suchus" meaning crocodile

facts.statement: Necrosuchus lived approximately 60 million years ago during the Paleocene epoch in what is now Argentina.
facts.quote: Necrosuchus is an extinct genus of caiman from modern day Argentina that lived during the Paleocene epoch (Danian or possibly Selandian age, about 60 million years ago)

facts.statement: Necrosuchus inhabited marine or river-lake environments within the Patagonian Salamanca Formation.
facts.quote: It inhabited the marine or fluvio-lacustrine environment of the Patagonian Salamanca Formation

facts.statement: Necrosuchus is distinguished from other caimans by having its 13th lower jaw tooth as the second largest, a trait shared only with Purussaurus brasiliensis and some Paleosuchus species.
facts.quote: The 13th tooth's status of second largerst tooth in the dentary differentiates Necrosuchus from all other caimans other than Purussaurus brasiliensis and some species of Paleosuchus

facts.statement: Evidence suggests the holotype specimen of Necrosuchus died before reaching full adult size, as indicated by unfused vertebrae sutures.
facts.quote: The sutures of the dorsal and sacral neurocentrals are unfused and still open, suggesting that the animal was not yet fully grown by the time of its death

facts.statement: Research indicates that Necrosuchus possesses derived features characteristic of alligatoroids, specifically within the subfamily Caimaninae.
facts.quote: Later research showed that Necrosuchus shows derived features of alligatoroids and more precisely caimanines

facts.statement: A 2020 study placed Necrosuchus as a derived member of Caimaninae, though its exact position remains uncertain due to a large polytomy involving modern caimans and Purussaurus.
facts.quote: Following a taxonomic revision and amended diagnosis published in 2020, Cicade and colleagues recovered Necrosuchus as a derived member of Caimaninae nested within a large polytomy with most extant non-paleosuchus caimans and Purussaurus

facts.statement: Necrosuchus is classified within the family Alligatoridae.
In phylogenetic analyses, Necrosuchus is often recovered as a parent group or close relative of the genus Jacarea.
The time range for Necrosuchus is estimated to be between 66 and 61.66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Danian to Danian (66 to 61.66 million years ago)
